                                                                                                  4EC127Q1
Q1     A metal spoon, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are placed in a saucepan of boiling water.
       If you feel the spoon handles 10 minutes later, the
       A        metal, plastic and wooden spoons will all be very hot.
       B        metal spoon will be hotter than the plastic and wooden spoons.
       C        plastic spoon will be hotter than the metal spoon.
       D        metal spoon will be colder than the wooden spoon.

                                                                                                  4EC127Q2


Q2     Explain the reason for your answer to Question 1.
       ________________________________________________________________
       ________________________________________________________________
       ________________________________________________________________




Copyright DEST 2004
 Hot handle                                                                                         4EC127

Scientific explanation for the teacher
Solids are made of particles that vibrate about fixed positions. When they are heated the
particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate more quickly. As the vibrating particles bump
into each other, the energy is passed along the solid from the hot end to the cold end.
Metals are better conductors of heat than wood or plastic; this is why they heat up
quickly and cool down quickly. When the spoons are placed in the hot water the heat is
conducted up the handles of the spoons. As the heat is conducted more quickly by metal
than by wood or plastic, the metal spoon will have a hotter handle than the plastic and
wooden spoons.

Student responses
    Typical student responses                                   Explanation
The metal has an attraction for heat.    These explanations are all misconceptions based on
Metal sucks up heat.                     beliefs that properties of metal enable it to hold or
Metals hold heat better.                 attract heat rather than carry heat from a hot end to a
                                         cold end.
The metal is a better conductor than     This scientific explanation shows that the student has
the others so the handle gets hot        recognised that properties of metals allow them to
quickly.                                 carry heat from a hot end to a cold end more quickly
                                         than plastic or wood.


Research findings
A review of research findings (Erickson & Tiberghien, 1985) in the area of heat and
temperature describes the range of ideas given by 4–13-year-olds.
In general, 8–9-year-olds describe heat as a ‘state of hotness’ along a continuum from
cold through warm to hot, while 8-12-year-olds tend to associate heat with living
objects, sources of heat, and the effect of heat on objects.


Conduction
Nearly all students are aware that one hot object is capable of ‘heating-up’ another
cooler object when they come into direct contact, e.g. a cool saucepan gets hot when
placed on a hot stove. Many students explain how metal gets hot faster than wood or
plastic by stating that a metal has an attraction for heat, and a tendency to hold heat.
Younger students (<13 years) tend to state that the strength of the object affects its
heating and so does the strength of the heat.

The types of questions that students were asked in regard to the conduction of heat
include:
1. Which materials are good for the thermal insulation of a house?
2. Which materials are good for the thermal insulation of a hot drink or of ice?
3. Why is the handle of a metal spoon hotter than the handle of a wooden or plastic
    spoon when they are placed in hot water?




Copyright DEST 2004
 Hot handle                                                                                 4EC127
Common explanations given by students are listed below.
 The material retains warmth or cold, better or less well.
 The material has the property to be cold or warm because of its nature.
 The material becomes hot or cold, more or less quickly.
 The material retains, lets in or lets out hot or cold air, better or less well.
 The material takes the temperature of its surroundings.
 The material is a conductor or an insulator.


Temperature
By 8 or 9 years of age, students think that temperature is related to levels of hotness.
Between ages 8 and 12 years, students are able to use and read a thermometer, but
may not apply this scientifically. Some pupils think that objects of different materials
in the same room are at different temperatures. They say that metal objects are colder
than wood–objects.

Temperature is also often related to size. More than 50% of 12-year-olds thought that
a larger ice cube would have a colder temperature than a smaller one, and hence the
large ice cube takes longer to melt.


Thermal equilibrium
Students also have difficulty with the fact that everyday objects heat up. Only 30% of
students, before instruction, think that the temperature of sand, sugar and water will
increase when they are heated. Students have difficulty with thermal equilibrium. If
several objects are in the same environment in prolonged contact, then they are at the
same temperature. Even though a metal plate and a plastic plate are on the same bench
most students consider that they are not at the same temperature. Similarly, different
materials (flour, nails, water) placed for several hours in an oven at 600C are said by
the majority of students to be at different temperatures. The reasons below are typical.
           Flour is at less than 600C because flour does not heat up very much.
           Nails are at more than 600C because the iron heats faster.
           Water is at 600C because it takes the temperature of the surroundings.
Of junior secondary students, 10% gave the correct answer before instruction and
30% gave the correct answer after instruction.


Teaching implications
Heat can be directly sensed by students, and comparisons between hot and cold can be
made by touching different objects. Objects that are sensed as hot are hotter than the
skin temperature, and substances sensed as cold are colder than skin temperature.
Touch gives a relative measure of hotness. If you place one hand on a metal plate at
room temperature and the other hand on a plastic plate at room temperature, even
though both plates are at the same temperature, the metal plate feels cooler because
the metal conducts heat away from the hand faster than the plastic plate. The use of
thermometers is essential to overcome errors of perception about the degree of
hotness. Many students will also consider heat and cold to be ‘substances’ that are in
various materials rather than the thermal energy of a material.




Copyright DEST 2004
 Hot handle                                                                                   4EC127
Misconceptions about metals being strong and attracting heat or holding heat can be
challenged by using lengths of wire with one end placed in hot water so that students
can feel the heat moving along the wire, i.e. conduction rather than attracting or
holding heat. Open discussions expose students to different explanations of these
phenomena so that alternative conceptions can be challenged, and help students
generalise their ideas to new examples and to appreciate their range of application.

References
Erickson, G., & Tiberghien, A. (1985). Heat and temperature. In R. Driver, E. Guesne & A. Tiberghien
       (Eds), Children's Ideas in Science (pp. 52–84). Buckingham: Open University Press.

CHAPTER 4: Compounds — Formulae and Naming

(a) COMPOUNDS CONTAINING ONLY NON-METALS

i) Most compounds containing only non-metals exist as molecules in which the
atoms are bound together by sharing electrons (covalent bonding).

Being molecular, the formula of each of these compounds indicates the composi-
tion of the molecules.

A few compounds containing onlv non-metals, such as silicon carbide and silicon
dioxide, exist as covalent network lattices. Thus the formula of each of these
compounds is just the simplest ratio of atoms in the lattice e.g. SiC and SiO,.

Naming compounds of two non-metals.

Unless common names are used, the name of a non-metal compound also tells us
he composition of the molecules, or the simplest ratio of atoms in the lattice; that is,
he formula is self evident from the name.

Rules for Naming

1. The name of the element closer to the bottom, left-hand corner of the periodic
table is given first.

2. The name of the second element is altered to end with the suffix “-ide”.

3. Prefixes are used to indicate the number of atoms of each element, except for the
case of only one atom of the first named element.

IONS
Atoms contain 3 types of particles: Protons, neutrons and electrons.




Sometimes electrons can be lost or gained by an atom.
When atoms loose or gain electrons they become charged.
There are two possible charges: positive or negative.
Positive = +
Negative = -
When atoms become charged we call them IONS.
Ions are charged particles.




When atoms lose electrons they become positive ions.
Metal atoms tend to lose electrons and become positive ions.

Eye
For concentrated complexities, no other organ in Joe's body can equal me. No larger than a Ping-Pong ball, I have tens of millions of
electrical connections and can handle 1.5 million simultaneous messages. I gather 80 percent of all the knowledge Joe absorbs. He
thinks of me as a miniature television camera. I consider the comparison insulting. I am much more sensitive than the biggest, costliest
TV camera ever made. I am responsible for one of the greatest of all miracles - sight.

Today's world is giving me a hard time. I was not built for it. For Joe's prehistoric ancestors, the eye's main job was to see things at a
distance danger to be avoided, game to be killed. Only lately have I been called on for continuous close-up work.

Look at my anatomy and you will understand why I am having difficulty adjusting to today's demands. First, my front window - my
clear, 20 cent size cornea. It starts the seeing process by bending light rays into orderly patterns. Next, my pupil - an adjustable gateway
for light. In bright sun it is nearly closed; on a dark night it is wide open. Up to this point there is nothing about seeing that a cheap
camera could not handle.

My wonders really begin with my lens-a little envelope of fluid the size and shape of an oval vitamin pill. My lens is surrounded by a
ring of tiny, superbly strong, unbelievably hard-working muscles. When they tense, my lens fattens for near vision; when they relax, it
flattens for distant vision. This was a fine arrangement for Joe's caveman ancestors. Since they were mainly interested in things six or
more meters away, the muscles were relaxed most of the time. But Joe now lives in a close-up world-lots of reading, deskwork and
such. This keeps my ciliary muscles tensed a lot of the time. They grow tired.
In front of and behind my lens I have two fluid-filled chambers In front the fluid is like water; in back it is about the consistency of
egg white. The watery fluid keeps me firmly inflated. Both fluids must be absolutely clear to permit passage of light. Those "specks"
Joe sees when he looks at a bright light are cellular remnants left over from his days in the womb when I was under construction.
They will float aimlessly in his eye fluid as long as he lives.

When Joe looks at some object, the light passes through my lens, which brings it into correct focus on my retina, a kind of onionskin
wallpaper, which covers the rear two thirds of my interior. Except in Joe's brain, I do not think that
anywhere else in his body is so much packed into so small a space. Covering less than three-square centimeters, my retina
contains 137 million light-sensitive receptor cells 130 million shaped like rods for black-and-white vision, seven million shaped like
cones for color vision.

The rods are scattered all over my retina. Let a firefly pass at night and a complex chemistry gets under way. The faint light bleaches
rhodopsin, a purplish-red pigment in my rods. The bleaching process generates a tiny wisp of electricity--a few millionths of a volt, far
 too little to tickle a mosquito. This feeds into my straw-size optic nerve and is transmitted to Joe's brain at about 450 km. per hour. The
brain interprets the signals flooding in and hands down its verdict: a firefly. All of this intricate electrochemical activity has been
completed in about .002 second!

If my rods seem complex, my cones are far more so. They are concentrated in the fovea, a pinhead size, and yellowish depression at
the rear of my chamber. This is the center for acute vision - reading, any close work--and for color. A leading theory is that these
cones, too, have bleachable pigments, one each for red, green and blue. Like an artist mixing paints on a palette, Joe's brain blends
these colors to make scores of other hues. If anything should go wrong with this intricate electrochemical process, Joe would be -
color-blind--as one in eight men is to some degree. In dim light, activity of my cones diminishes, color sense vanishes and every thing
becomes gray, as my rods take over.

While Joe sees with me, he sees in his brain. A crushing blow at the back of his head, severe enough to destroy the optical center of his
brain, would produce permanent blindness. A lesser blow and he sees “stars” - a chaotic electrical disturbance. Joe gets clinching
evidence of the brain's role when he dreams. He "sees" pictures, even with my lids closed in total darkness. Had he been born blind, he
would dream in terms of other sensory stimuli: touch, sound, even smell.

Joe was not born with the eyes he has today. At birth he could see only light and shadow. In the first few months he was farsighted,
like his caveman ancestors. To study his rattle, he held it as far as possible from his face. At first, Joe's eyes were poorly coordinated;
I would wander in one direction, my partner in another. Our wandering worried Joe's mother. It
should not have. A few months after birth we were moving in exact unison. By the time Joe was six, his vision was excellent.
But my peak sight did not come until age eight.

When he was young, Joe used to read in dim light. His mother warned that he was "ruining" his eyes. Nonsense. The young see
better in dim light than adults; and viewing under even the most adverse circumstances does no harm.

I have a number of other unusual attributes. Tiny though they are, my muscles, milligram for milligram, are among the body's
strongest. In an average day, I move about 100,000 times - to bring objects into sharp focus. Joe would have to walk 80km to give
his leg muscles similar exercise.

My cleaning equipment is similarly striking. My lacrimal glands produce a steady stream of moisture--tears to flush away dust and
other foreign material. My eyelids, of course, act as windshield wipers. Joe blinks three to six times a minute- more when I am tired.
This keeps my cornea moist and clean. The tears also contain a potent microbe-killer called lysozyme, which guards me from infective
bacteria.
 I try to ward off fatigue by resting as much as possible. I get time oh when Joe blinks. And my partner and I spell each other for a
while I may carry 90 percent of the work load, while Joe's other eye loafs; then it goes to work and I rest.

Nature gave me superb protection, placing me in a bony cavern with protruding cheekbones and forehead to act as shock absorbers
for direct blows. She also gave me supersensitive nerves to activate the alarm if there should be a potentially damaging intruder such
as cinder.

Still, I do have my troubles. My focusing apparatus often fails to work perfectly. Eyeglasses can correct 95 percent of this trouble.
Disease is a more serious problem. One potential disorder is really a plumbing problem either too much fluid entering me or too little
draining away. Pressure builds up, reducing the blood supply to my optic nerve. This is
glaucoma.

In severe instances, glaucoma can cause permanent blindness in a few days. More often it is a leisurely performer, producing
symptoms so mild they are apt to go unnoticed. These symptoms: colored halos around bright lights, loss of side vision, difficulty in
adjusting to the dark, a blurring of vision. At his age, Joe has one chance in 40 of glaucoma damaging his sight or blinding him
completely. His doctor can check for glaucoma simply by pressing a little gadget called a tonometer against my eyeball. Joe should
have this test every year. The treatment for glaucoma? Drugs in drop
form, or surgery.

Astigmatism is another of my common ailments. In this one, my cornea is not a spherical surface and distorts vision like a bubble flaw
in a piece of glass. Eyeglasses correct this condition A detached retina is more serious. It occurs when my retinal wallpaper blisters or
peels, and usually announces itself with flashing lights, image distortion blurring spots. A surgeon can "tack" my wallpaper back in
place with 80 percent chance of success.

Both my cornea and my lens-normally totally transparent tissue--can cloud and lead to blindness. If it is the cornea, Joe can re gain
sight with a corneal transplant. If it is the lens, he will need a cataract operation, and either thick eyeglasses or contact lenses
afterward.

Fortunately, Joe has so far escaped all these things. Just the same, I am growing old--like Joe's other organs. The transparency of my
lens is lower, accommodation muscles are weaker, hardened arteries are diminishing blood supply to my retina. These processes will
continue, but Joe should not worry unduly. The odds are heavily in favor of my providing him with serviceable vision as long as he
lives.

Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                      1




                                 Light Energy
If you can read this, you are relying on light energy. Light energy and our eyesight are the
two things we need to be able to see; without one or the other there would be no sight.
Can you imagine what life would be like without light energy? Quite simply, there would
not be any life at all. Plants need light to live and if there were no plants, there would be no
animals, including people.


Sources of Light

Light energy is one of the forms of radiant energy that comes to us from
the Sun. This light energy is formed in nuclear reactions that occur within the Sun.
Other objects and substances can also give off their own light energy. These objects
are said to be luminous. The light carries energy away from luminous objects as
electromagnetic waves.

1.        Give examples of objects or substances that are luminous.




Many light sources emit light energy because they are hot. However, there are light sources which give out light without
getting hot. These include fluorescent tubes, the paint on the hand and numerals of clocks, fireflies and some deep sea
fish.

3.        Draw energy flow charts to show where the light energy comes from for the following objects:
          a)        a candle


          b)        a torch


          c)        an electric light bulb

          not produce their own light.

                    b) Explain why the Moon shines brightly in the night sky.

How light travels

One scientific theory proposes that light energy travels in a wave motion. The light that we
can see has a wavelength of about th of a millimetre. Light energy travels at a speed of about
300 million metres per second.

example, light will travel in a straight line unless some other substance is placed in its path.

When light energy hits an object, several different things can happen. What happens depends on the substance making up
the object. Some substances allow light energy to pass through them. Other substances will not allow light energy to
pass through and either reflect (bounce off) or absorb the energy.

bounce off the object enable us to see it.

           reflects the light from an object and makes the image which we see.

           observations:

           The image is     the same size as or smaller than or larger than        the word written on the paper.
           The letters and word in the image are    the same as    or reversed compared to the word written on the
            paper.

 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Light Energy                                                                       5




Absorption and reflection of light

Although sunlight appears to be white, it is not actually a single pure white colour. It is made up of seven different
colours that you can see, called the visible spectrum. The colours of the visible spectrum are red, orange, yellow, green,
indigo and violet. Each of these colours correspond to light of different wavelengths with red light having the longest
wavelength and violet light having the shortest wavelength.

Different materials absorb some of the colours in sunlight (white light) and reflect others. The colour we see in an object
depends on the colours that are reflected back to our eyes. For example, a yellow object absorbs all colours except
yellow, and it reflects yellow.

White objects appear white because they reflect all the colours of sunlight, but black objects appear black because they
absorb all the colours and reflect none.


9.        Using coloured pens or pencils, colour and complete the following diagrams, showing the colour of the leaf and
of        the bananas, and the different colours in the sunlight (white light) and in the reflected light.

Bending of light

10.       Place a coin in an empty cup and move your eyes until it is just out
          of view. Ask your partner to carefully fill the cup with water.
                   What happens to the coin?




11.       Put a pencil in a beaker of water. Look at the pencil from the side of the beaker. What do you see?




When light energy meets a new substance, the light changes direction or bends. When light bends going from one
substance to another, we say that the light is refracted. The light bends when going from one substance to another
because it moves at different speeds through different materials. It travels slower through water and glass than it does
through air.

 This means that if a green light and a red light of equal intensity shine towards you,
you will see the green light as being brighter. The luminous intensity of a source,
measured in a unit called the candela, takes into account the sensitivity of a typical
person’s vision to different wavelengths of light. For example, an incandescent 60 W
globe appears to have the same luminous intensity as a 9 W compact fluorescent
globe. This happens because the incandescent globe emits a lot of heat radiation
and less of the colours of the spectrum that the eye is sensitive to compared to the
compact fluorescent. (Note that 1 candela is very roughly equal to the light produced
by one large candle.)

A light meter measures the illuminance of a source, using a unit called the lux. The
illuminance of a source is a measure of the intensity of light falling on a surface per
unit area. The approximate illuminance (in lux) of a number of sources is shown in

METALS AND NON-METALS and the PERIODIC TABLE


Elements are arranged on the periodic table due to their properties. Two big groupings are the metals
and the non-metals. Metals all share certain properties.

                       PROPERTIES OF METALS AND NON-METALS
Metals

    • Capable of being highly polished (they have a lustre or are
      shiny when cut).
    • Good conductors of heat and electricity.
    • All are solid at room temperature (except for mercury).
    • Can be hammered into thin sheets (malleable) and
      stretched into wires (ductile).
Non-metals

      • Usually don't shine when polished.
      • Poor conductors of electricity (except carbon), and heat.
      • Exist as solids, liquids and gases at room temperature.
      • Those that are solid are brittle (they shatter).

Metalloids
This group have some metal properties and some non-metal properties.

Mirrors and Lenses

Ray diagrams in a plane mirror
Ray diagrams are used to show an image of an object reflected in a mirror. Straight lines from the object are
drawn towards the mirror. Using the rule from the angle of incidence and reflection the lines are then reflected
back. Arrows are used on the lines to show the light rays’ direction.

The main rule for mirrors is that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.




                                                                           This means that the angle of the light ray
                                                                           between where it arrives and the
                                                                           perpendicular line called the normal, to
                                                                           where it hits on the surface of the mirror
                                                                           is the same angle it leaves and the same
                                                                           perpendicular (normal) line.




Convex and concave mirrors
Mirrors work because light is reflected from them. The three types of mirrors are:




The images in the plane mirrors are the same size, the right way up but laterally inverted (changed right to left)
and is a flat reflecting surface.

The images in the concave mirror are
   a) magnified and the right way up when you are near to the mirror
   b) smaller and upside down when you are further away from the mirror
The images in the convex mirror are reduced and the right way up

 Ray diagrams in a concave mirror

                                                        With concave mirrors, light being reflected converges
                                                        (goes in an inward direction) towards the focal point
                                                        (x). From a distance, images appear upside down but
                                                        when brought nearer, image become larger in size
                                                        and appears right side up. A focal point is where
                                                        parallel rays meet.




Ray diagrams in a convex mirror

The image formed in a convex mirror is always
upright and smaller in size. The light rays
diverge (spread apart). The focal point is behind
the mirror where light rays do not actually pass
through.

Refraction

A glass or plastic lens is transparent. This means that
light can be transmitted through the object without the
light being absorbed.

The medium of a plastic or glass lens has a different
optical density to air. Light rays entering the lens are
refracted to a different angle.

Refraction is when light travels between two optically
different (densities) mediums that bend light towards
or away from the normal.
Refraction in a glass block
                                       The ray of light bends or refracts inwards when it moves into the
                                       glass. This makes the angle of refraction smaller than the angle of
                                       incidence.

                                       When the ray emerges from the glass back into the air then it
                                       continues on a parallel path to the original ray.


                                       A medium is any space or substance which will allow light to travel
                                       through it called transmission. Examples of different media include
                                       air, water and glass. Each medium has different optical density. The
                                       optical density of a medium affects the speed at which light rays
                                       travel through. When a light ray passes from one medium into
                                       another (e.g. from air into water) it will change direction where two
                                       media meet. This ‘bending’ of light is called refraction and it always
                                       occurs when the two media have different optical densities.

Observation – Inference – Prediction

Purpose: To practice distinguishing between observations, inferences and predictions.

Scientists spend a great deal of time observing the natural and built world. When a scientists observes he or
she takes in information using the five senses. Often tools such as microscopes are used to extend the senses
and make the observations more precise and accurate.

Observations may be qualitative or quantitative. Qualitative observations are those that describe qualities,
properties or characteristics of objects or phenomena. Color, texture, smells, sounds are all examples of
qualitative observations. Quantitative observations are those that can be measured in numbers. Mass,
volume, speed, temperature are a few examples. Tools are often used to make quantitative observations.

Observations in science should always be facts (a statement that can be proven true or false), not opinions (an
expression of a person’s feelings that cannot be proven).

Observations lead to inferences. An inference is an educated guess or reasonable conclusion drawn from the
observation. It is a possible explanation for the observation.

Predictions can be made from inferences. A scientific prediction is an educated guess about a future event. It
can be made without knowing whether it is correct; it may be an incorrect guess. That’s ok. Scientists learn
from incorrect guesses as much as correct ones.

For example, a student wakes up to thunder one morning.
He may observe the thunder – using his sense of hearing, he made a factual, qualitative observation.
The sound of the thunder led to the inference that it was raining – it might not have been raining.
The student then predicted that they would not go outside during school that day because of the rain.

The Particle Theory of Matter
Matter

There are thousands of different sorts of materials, all with their own special
characteristics that make them suitable for particular uses. While they are all
different, they all have one thing in common: they are all made of matter.

Matter is defined as anything that has mass (can be weighed) and volume
(takes up space). Objects and materials are matter. Things that are not
matter include time, heat and gravity. A space that does not contain any
matter at all is called a vacuum. Outer space is very close to a perfect
vacuum.

The Particle Theory of Matter

In the particle model, matter is described as being made up of very small
particles which are constantly moving. Scientists have built up this model
by performing investigations and making observations of the behaviour of
different types of matter.

Below are three example of evidence for the particle model.

Brownian Motion

In 1827, Robert Brown first investigated pollen grains in
water. He selected pollen because it is very light. Brown
observed that the pollen grains were constantly moving
around in a random manner. The particle model can be used to explain these
observations. The particles that make up the water are constantly moving and
bump into the pollen grains causing them to change direction. This type of
movement was named Brownian motion, after Robert Brown.

Diffusion

Your nose is very sensitive to particles. Small particles move into your nose
through the air and are detected by sensitive membranes. Being able to smell
                                someone’s perfume or something baking in the
                                oven from a distance are examples of particles
                                moving through the air into your nose. The
                                movement of small particles through a
                                substance, such as air or water, is called
                                diffusion. The particles bump into each other,
                                constantly changing directions and mixing until
                                they are spread out fairly evenly. The figure on
the left shows the diffusion of particles of ammonia in air.

Dissolving
 Substances such as sugar can dissolve when put into water. Dissolving can be
explained in terms of small particles moving through the water particles. This
movement can be sped up by stirring, which forces the particles to move in the
water faster.

Chapter 7                                      Elements
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1:                          Properties of water
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                     VERBAL/LINGUISTIC, VISUAL/SPATIAL


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________

Water is one of the most common compounds on Earth. It covers 71% of the Earth’s
surface and makes up over 50% of your body. It is easy to forget that water has
some very special properties that are unlike any other compound. Without these
special properties, life as we know it could not exist.


Melting and boiling points of water
Water is one of the only compounds that you can see as a solid, liquid or gas at
temperatures commonly found on Earth. In your kitchen you can find water as a solid
(ice cubes), liquid (water from the tap) and gas (steam from a kettle or humidity in the
air).

In fact, the melting and boiling points of water were used to define the Celsius
temperature scale. The melting point of water at sea level was used to define 0C in
the Celsius scale. The boiling point of water at sea level was used to define 100C.


Density of water
Another unusual property of water is that its solid form (ice) is less dense than its
liquid form (liquid water). As a result, ice floats in water. This is something you can
see with ice cubes in a drink or icebergs on the ocean. However, this property is
actually quite unusual. Most substances are more dense in the solid form and so sink
to the bottom of the liquid.




        Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 Water is most dense at 4C (four degrees above its freezing point). This unusual
property of water is of critical importance to aquatic (water dwelling) plant and animal
life in cold climates. It means that water at 4C sinks to the bottom of a lake and water
at 0C floats to the top. As a result, lakes freeze from the top down. This allows plants
and animals in the lake to continue living, foraging and breeding in the lakebed.


The universal solvent
Water is also very good at dissolving a large range of substances. For this reason,
water is sometimes referred to as ‘the universal solvent’. This term is slightly
misleading because water cannot dissolve all substances (for example, oil, gold,
chalk). Still, water is a very important solvent and is used to make solutions of most
of the compounds you use in the laboratory.


Questions
1   List other substances that you find in your everyday life that can be commonly
    found in two or more states and fill in the table below. Can you think of any

Safety With Electricity

                                          Answers

1   The pool could have been placed out of bounds while work around the pool was in progress.

2   More electrical shocks were experienced in summer because more portable appliances were
    used outdoors, people were more likely to be barefooted and people tried to fix their own
    appliances.

3   The hair drier would be carrying a current and this would be transferred to the water in the
    bath. If a person was in the bath they would conduct the current through their body and
    receive an electrical shock.

4   Water which is not pure is a good conductor of electricity. If water (dampness) is
    surrounding electrical appliances or cables it will conduct the current to anyone who touches
    the appliance or cord.

Book 2: Safety & equipment
    in the laboratory

Name:            Block:
                          1
    1.   Students are not to enter the lab (ie: be at lab benches with lab materials) unless a teacher is present.
       Students are NEVER to enter the lab prep room.

  2. Never run or ‘muck around’ in the laboratory. During a lab, you MUST remain at your own bench.

  3. There is no food or drink permitted in the laboratory. At desks is OK.

  4. Water bottles & bags/backpacks are to be left at your desk during labs.

  5. NEVER taste or smell any substance in the lab, unless instructed to do so safely by your teacher.

  6. Always listen carefully and follow instructions specifically. If there is anything you don’t understand, ask
       your teacher. It is very important for your safety that you understand all instructions.

  7. Always clean up and return equipment to the correct place when finished an experiment.

  8. Keep benches and floor areas tidy. This means all chairs must be pushed in when working at the lab
       benches, and extra books/equipment is never to be placed on the floor.

  9. Breaks and accidents (even minor) must always be reported to your teacher immediately.

  10. NEVER attempt to pick up broken glass. Inform your teacher, and keep others clear of the area.

  11. Laboratory equipment and chemicals are ONLY to be used as directed by your teachers’ instructions.

  12. Waste products/remains from experiments are to be disposed of as instructed by your teacher. Remember,
       not everything is safe to rinse down the sink, or throw away in the bin.

  13. Be sure any burning material (eg. Match) is put out completely before throwing away.

  14. All hot equipment is to be placed to a heatproof mat, NOT directly on the benchtop.

  15. ALWAYS wear safety glasses during experiments with hazardous materials or when heating.

  16. Long hair and loose clothing must be tied back during experiments.

  17. Long pants & closed toed shoes must be worn during experiments

  18. ALWAYS wash your hands after any experiments in the laboratory.

  19. Use gas taps & water for EXPERIMENTS only.

  20. Bench tops are to be cleaned and disinfected following EVERY practical experiment.

  21. When heating or mixing substances, NEVER point towards yourself or others.

  22. Never mix chemicals or do your own experiments unless you have permission from your teacher. This is
       wasteful, and could be very dangerous.

  23. Always rinse/clean glassware following an experiment.

  24. Always use tongs to pick up equipment/objects that have been heated

  25. If you need to leave a Bunsen Burner, ALWAYS turn it to the visible orange/yellow safety flame

Misbehaviour & breach of safety rules in the laboratory will result in immediate consequences, including
                       a ban from participation in any further practical experiments.

Safety With Electricity
Below are two press articles which refer to electrical safety. Read the articles and answer
the questions which follow. You may need to refer to other sources for some of the
answers.


Schoolgirl Dies
An 11-year-old Sydney schoolgirl has died from injuries received in a pool accident which also killed her
best friend. A spokesman for Westmead Hospital said she died early yesterday morning. She never
recovered from receiving electric shocks in a swimming pool on 19 December. Her friend, also 11, died
later that same day. A live wire came into contact with the water in which the two girls were swimming
after the pool filter's electrical cable was accidentally cut.

The Age, 27 December 1988


Electrical Shocks More Likely in Summer
By DAVID THOMSON

People are twice as likely to suffer electrical shocks in summer as in the rest of the year, the SEC
has warned.
  A survey of the number of shocks reported in the 10 years to 1986 found that 65 per cent of
them occurred between October and March, the SEC's acting Victorian Chief Electrical
Inspector, Mr Ian Graham, said.
   He said the risk increased in summer because portable appliances were used outdoors and in
tents and caravans, people were barefooted or near water, especially pools, and people tried to do
their own electrical repairs and installations.
   Mr Graham said 500 electrical shocks had been reported to the SEC last year. There had been
another 100 cases in council supplied areas. About one-tenth of all shocks were the result of
dampness.
    He said there had been 17 fatalities from electrical appliances in 1987. There have been two
deaths from electrical contact with swimming pools since wiring regulations were revised in
1976 to isolate electrical equipment, including earthing and lighting, from pools.
   Mr Graham said checking existing electrical fittings was much more difficult than issuing
guidelines for new works.
   "We cannot check every single pool in Melbourne; we do not have the right to interfere."
    Mr Graham said pool owners should check permanently wired electrical fittings such as
pumps and underwater lights. Variations in water levels and heat caused power lines to sag,
which was dangerous where they crossed water.
    He said there had been a number of fatalities caused by hair dryers falling into baths. Mr
Graham said people should remember that it was illegal and unsafe for unlicensed tradesmen to
work on fixed wiring of houses, and that caution was needed with extension cords to tents and
caravans.

Questions

         avoided ?

2        List the reasons why it is more likely that more electric shocks are experienced in
         summer.

3        How could a hair drier falling into a bath cause a fatality ?

4        Why would dampness contribute to a large number of electrical shocks ?

Introduction to the Scientific Method Worksheet
Long ago, many people believed that living things could come from nonliving things.
They thought that worms came from wood and that maggots came from decaying
meat. This idea was called
spontaneous generation. In 1668,
an Italian biologist, Francesco Redi,
did experiments to prove that
maggots did not come from meat.
One of his experiments is shown
below.


Redi placed pieces of meat in
several jars. He divided the jars into
two groups. He covered the first
group of jars with fine cloth. He left the second group of jars uncovered. Redi
observed the jars for several days. He saw flies on the cloth of the covered jars, and
he saw flies laying eggs on the meat in the uncovered jars. Maggots appeared only
on the meat in the group of jars left uncovered.

Questions
1. Which is not a step in the scientific method?
      a. Problem or question.                    c. Ask other people for their opinion.
      b. Research.                               d. Arrive at a conclusion.

2. What was the problem in Redi’s experiment?
      a. How do maggots appear in meats?
      b. How do worms appear in wood?
      c. Is spontaneous generation a valid explanation for maggots in meats?
      d. All of the above are examples of problems.

3. What do you think his hypothesis was?
      a. Maggots grow through spontaneous generation.
      b. Maggots come from eggs laid by flies.
      c. Maggots find their way into woods and meats.
      d. The problem cannot be solved.

4. How did he test his hypothesis?
      a. He placed food in two jars, covering one jar and leaving the other
uncovered.
      b. He placed food in two jars and left both jars uncovered.
      c. He placed food in two jars and covered both jars.
      d. He put food in one jar and no food in a second jar.

5. What was the variable in his experiment?
      a. Covering both jars.
      b. Covering one jar and leaving the other uncovered.
      c. Leaving both jars uncovered.
      d. There was no variable in this experiment.

6. What do you think Redi’s conclusion was?
      a. Living things come from other living things.
      b. Living things are created through spontaneous generation.
      c. He did not have enough data to arrive at a conclusion.

The Scientific Method Homework and Study Guide	
  
                                        Teacher Answer Key

Define the following terms:

1. data: The information gathered from making observations.

2. independent variable: The variable that is deliberately changed by the scientist.

3. dependent variable: The variable observed during the experiment. It is the data collected as a result of
   changing the independent variable.

4. scientific method: A series of steps used by scientists to solve a problem or answer a question.

Short Answer:
1. List the steps to the scientific method.

           1) Observe / Ask a question.
           2) Form a hypothesis.
           3) Design a controlled experiment.
           4) Record and analyze the results.
           5) Draw a conclusion.

2. How is a theory different from a hypothesis?

       A hypothesis is an “educated guess” that is testable through observations and experimentation. A theory is a
       broad statement of what is believed to be true based on many experiments and considerable amounts of data.

3. Give two examples of quantitative data.

       There are many possible answers. Any type of answer that is “numerical” should be accepted. Possibilities
       might include: Number of students who failed a particular test. The amount of weight gain by mice when
       fed a particular diet.

4. Give two examples of qualitative data.

       There are many possible answers. Any type of answer that is “descriptive” should be accepted.
       Possibilities might include: Starch turns purple in the presence of iodine. During mating season, male bird
       plumage becomes bright and colorful.

5. How many variables should an experiment test at a time? Explain your answer.

       Only one variable can be tested at a time. If several variables were changed at the same time, the scientist
       would not know which variable was responsible for the observed results.

6. Why is it important that scientists communicate and report their findings?

       In order for the findings to be considered “valid”, the experiment must be repeated by other scientists so that
       the results may be verified and corroborated.                                             Copyright

                                                                                                                               5	
  
 7. A drug company is testing the effectiveness of a new blood pressure medicine using rats as the test subjects.
    a) Describe the experimental group: The experimental group will consist of a set number of rats that will
                                          be given the new blood pressure medicine.


       b) Describe the control group: The control group will consist of a set number of rats that will not receive
                                      the new blood pressure medicine.


       c) What is the independent variable? The administering or not administering of the blood pressure
                                            medicine.


       d) What is the dependent variable? The observed changes in blood pressure of the test subjects.


       e) What are some possible factors that must remain constant during the testing?
          All rats should be fed the same diet and in the same quantity.
          All rats should be kept at the same stress level.
          All rats should be housed in the same type of cages.
          All rats should be kept at the same temperature.
          The rats should be all of one species.


       f) What is the ONE factor that will be different between the experimental group and the control group?
          Whether or not the rats receive the new blood pressure medicine.


8. What is meant by the term “controlled experiment”?
   In a “controlled experiment” only one variable is changed at a time. All other variables should be
   unchanged or “controlled.”



9. Why must experiments be repeated many times?
   Experiments are repeated in order to see that the same results are obtained each time. Results cannot be
   considered “valid” until it is determined that the experiment will always yield the same conclusion.

Sight, Sound and Colour

Structure and Function of the human ear



                                                               Sound waves travel through the ear canal and
                                                               cause the eardrum to vibrate. The small bones
                                                               of the inner ear transfer this vibration to the
                                                               inner ear cochlea.

                                                               The cochlea is fluid filled and lined with many
                                                               hair-like nerve cells. Different length nerve cells
                                                               detect different wave frequencies and transmit
                                                               this information to the brain using electrical
                                                               impulses that move along the nerves.

Audible range of humans and other animals

Humans can hear between 20 – 20,000 Hertz, a measure of frequency. The frequency of a wave is calculated by
the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time.

In comparison to many other animals, humans have a very limited audible range. Bats and dolphins can hear
and produce sound at an exceedingly high frequency – and use it to bounce back off objects as sonar to “see”
without light. Low rumbling noises of elephants and moles are below our auditory range but can travel long
distances.




Pitch and Loudness of sound

                                                           Sound can be described by “characteristics”
                                                           called pitch and loudness. Pitch is related to
                                                           frequency – the higher the frequency then
                                                           the higher the pitch of the note (a single
                                                           sound at a particular level). Loudness is
                                                           related to amplitude – the higher the
                                                           amplitude the louder the sound.



105 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Reflecting sound waves

Sonar (originally an acronym for SOund Navigation And Ranging) is simply making use of an echo. When an
animal or machine makes a noise, it sends sound waves into the environment around it. Those waves bounce
off nearby objects, and some of them reflect to the object that made the noise. Whales and specialised machines
can use reflected waves to locate distant objects and sense their shape and movement.




Structure of the Human eye
                                                         The human eye is a “collecting” organ that allows light
                                                         to reach sensory nerves which then transmit electrical
                                                         signals to the brain. The convex lens focuses the images
                                                         seen onto the retina of the eye. Various sensory cells in
                                                         the retina called rods and cones detect both amount of
                                                         light and colour of light. The iris opens to let more light
                                                         into the eye when it is dimmer. The muscles around the
                                                         lens change the shape of the lens. The blind spot is the
                                                         point of entry of the optic nerve on the retina and has
                                                         no light receptors. The cornea is the tough transparent
                                                         layer at the front of the eye.

                                                         Messages from the retina travel through the optic nerve
                                                         to the brain. The brain further processes the images in
                                                         various parts of the brain responsible for language,
                                                         speech and thinking.


White light is made from colours mixed together
                                                 White light is a combination of all the other colours of light mixed
                                                 together. The main colours that make up white light can be seen
                                                 in a rainbow. They are red, orange, red, green, blue, indigo (a dark
                                                 inky blue) and violet. They can be remembered by the acronym
                                                 ROY G BIV.

                                                 The sun releases visible light of all wavelengths, when combined
                                                 becomes white light. When this white light hits the surface of a
                                                 red apple all the other colours of light except red are absorbed.
                                                 The red light is instead reflected, and when hitting our eyes, we
                                                 see the apple as red because that is the only wavelength
                                                 detected.
106 | P a g e    GZ Science Resources
 We see colours because of what wavelengths are reflected
A colour is a property processed by an object as
a result of the way it reflects, absorbs or emits
light of a specific wave length.

We see a tree as green because the leaves absorb
the red and blue light waves, and only the green
light is reflected into our eyes.




Prisms work by diffracting colours of different wavelengths
                                                    A prism is a triangular block used to disperse
                                                    white light. This causes light of different colours to
                                                    be refracted differently and to leave the prism at
                                                    different angles, creating an effect like a rainbow.
                                                    The degree of bending of the light's path varies
                                                    with the wavelength or colour of the light used,
                                                    called dispersion. This can be used to separate a
                                                    beam of white light into its spectrum of colours.


Primary and Secondary colours

 Combining light colours is said to be
 additive. Each wavelength of light
 adds to another.

 The three main colours of light are
 called primary. Two primary colours
 together make a secondary colour
 and all three primary colours
 together make up white light.

 NOTE: Paint absorbs light waves. The
 paint is called subtractive because
 with each addition of colour more of
 the wave lengths are absorbed. The
 three primary colours of paint are
 cyan, yellow and magenta. When
 these three are added together the
 resulting colour is black: all the
 different wavelengths of coloured
 light are absorbed.

Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Sound Energy                                                                        1




                                                   Sound Energy
Vibrations and Pitch

Sound occurs when something vibrates. Something vibrates when it moves back and forth very
quickly.

The highness or lowness of a sound is called the pitch.

1.        In the following three activities, sound energy is transformed from other types of energy:
                    i) flicking a ruler held on the edge of a desk
                    ii) gently blowing across the top of a straw
                    iii) gently tapping the side of a beaker with a glass rod

Experiment with sound energy in each of these three ways and then answer the following
questions.
         a)      What is vibrating to produce the sound?
                    i)
                    ii)
                    iii)

          b)        What energy transformations occurred during the production of sound in each of the three activities?
                    i)
                    ii)
                    iii)

          c)        How can you produce a sound of higher pitch in each of the three activities?
                    i)
                    ii)
                    iii)

2.        What feature of each of the following three musical instruments is changed to play a higher
          pitched note?

          a) a single string of a guitar
          b) a recorder
          c) a xylophone


How does sound move?

If a tuning fork is struck, it vibrates. When the prongs of the fork move forward, energy is transferred from the prongs to
the air particles and the particles are pushed closer together to form a patch of compressed air. Once formed, this area of
compression moves through the air as the particles collide with other particles and pass their energy on. This causes a
travelling vibration which is called a sound wave.
 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Sound Energy                                                                           2




                                                     vibration through the air




When the vibrations reach the ear drum, it is made to vibrate in step with the tuning fork. The vibrating ear drum passes
its energy on to smaller parts in the ear which finally results in electrical signals being transferred to the brain. The sound
is then heard.




The layers of compressed air produced by a vibrating object behave rather like the coils of a "slinky" spring.

Experiment with a spring, as suggested in the following diagram, to produce compressions which move like sound energy
moves through the air. Such travelling compressions are called longitudinal waves.




How fast sound energy is being transferred can be determined by measuring the number of
vibrations produced per second. This is called the frequency of the sound wave.
The frequency of a sound wave determines the pitch of the sound. Low notes have a small
frequency and high notes have large frequency.

Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 vibration per second.

3.        Make models of high and low note waves with the spring.

          Sketch what each spring looks like for the high note model and for the low
          note model in the table on the next page. Also complete the gaps.

          a)        What frequencies of sound energy can humans hear?


          b)        Name several other animals which can hear different frequencies of sound energy compared to
                    humans. Give the range of frequencies they can hear.




Echoes

5.        a)        What happens when the compressions in the spring reach the
                    fixed end of the spring?



          b)        What scientific name is given to this behaviour?

          c)        What is an echo?


          d)        What causes an echo?




Loudness

The loudness of a sound depends on how much energy goes into producing the vibration. A large
amount of energy will cause a loud sound and a smaller amount of energy will cause a soft sound.

6.        a)        What unit is used to measure sound level (degree of loudness)?


          b)        Name a soft sound and a loud sound, and their respective sound levels.



          c)        What sound levels can damage hearing? Compare this level to that
                    of a rock band.
 Year 8 Science - Energy & Change - Sound Energy                                                      4




What can sound travel through?

Usually sounds come to us as vibrations in the air, but we can also hear sounds that
vibrate through other materials, as long as they can make our eardrums vibrate.
Sound travels better through some materials than others.

                    iv) Hold a bell under water and ring it.

uploads/science/WK-The Particle Theory a.searchText:
The Particle Theory and States of Matter
 Matter is everything that has mass and takes up space.
 All matter is made up of tiny particles of atoms or molecules.
 The way the particles move and behave depends on the state or
  phase of the matter.
 The particles in matter are in constant motion. This is known as the
  Kinetic Theory.
 The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.

Particles in a Solid
 The particles are packed together tightly, with only small spaces
  between them.
 The particles are held together by strong forces so they cannot move
  freely, but vibrate around fixed positions.
 Solids expand when heated and contract when cooled.
 Solids have a fixed shape and volume.
 Solids cannot be compressed.

Particles in a Liquid
 The particles are packed tightly together, with only small spaces
  between them.
 The particles are held together by weaker forces, but they cannot
  move freely. They are able to roll over each other. This allows liquids
  to flow and be poured.
 Liquids expand when heated and contract when cooled.
 Liquids have no fixed shape but have a fixed volume.
 Liquids cannot be compressed.

Particles in a Gas
 The particles in gases are far apart and only held together with very
  weak forces.
 The particles are able to move freely in all directions.
 Gases have no fixed shape or volume but will fill up the container they
  are enclosed in.
 Gases will expand a lot when heated and shrink when cooled.
 Gases can become liquids if cooled or compressed enough.
 Temperature and Energy
 The temperature of a substance is a measure of the amount of
  internal energy the substance has.
 A substances state of matter is determined by its internal energy or
  temperature.
 Heating matter gives its particles more energy so they vibrate faster
  and move further apart. The matter will expand slightly in volume.
 If enough energy is put into the matter, the particles will have enough
  energy to overcome the forces holding them together and change
  phase.
 Cooling matter takes energy away from the particles so they vibrate
  more slowly and move closer together or shrinks in volume.
 When cooling takes enough energy out of the matter, the particles will
  move more slowly until they condense and change phase.

6. What is the relationship between particle movement and
   temperature?

     a. Solid turns to liquid
     b. Gas turns to liquid
     c. Liquid turns to gas
     d. Liquid turns to solid

The Speed of Sound:

 Sound travels at different speeds depending on what it is traveling through.
Of the three mediums (gas, liquid, and solid) sound waves travel the slowest
through gases, faster through liquids, and fastest through solids.
Temperature also affects the speed of sound.
Medium=

Molecules=

Properties=

Collide=

Magnitude=

Rapidly=

Obstacles=

Effectively=

Ocean dwelling=

Majority=

Gases:
The speed of sound depends upon the properties of the medium it is passing
through. When we look at the properties of a gas, we see that only when
molecules collide with each other can a sound wave move. So, it makes
sense that the speed of sound has the same order of magnitude as the
average molecular speed between collisions. In a gas, it is important to know
the temperature. This is because at lower temperatures, molecules collide
more often, giving the sound wave more chances to move around rapidly. At
freezing (0º Celcius), sound travels through air at 331 meters per second
(about 740 mph). But, at 20ºC, room temperature, sound travels at 343
meters per second (767 mph).
Liquids:
Sound travels faster in liquids than in gases because molecules are more
tightly packed. In fresh water, sound waves travel at 1,482 meters per
 second (about 3,315 mph). That's well over 4 times faster than in air! Many
ocean-dwelling animals rely upon sound waves to communicate with other
animals and to locate food and obstacles. The reason that they are able to
effectively use this method of communication over long distances is that
sound travels so much faster in water.
Solids:
Sound travels fastest through solids. This is because molecules in a solid
medium are much closer together than those in a liquid or gas, allowing
sound waves to travel more quickly through it. In fact, sound waves travel
over 17 times faster through steel than through air. The exact speed of
sound in steel is 5,960 meters per second (13,332 mph)! But, this is only for
the majority of solids. The speed of sound in all solids are not faster than in
all liquids.


Sound travels faster in a liquid than in a gas
because the particles are ____________ together in a
liquid.
Sound travels faster in a solid than a liquid because
the particles are _________ together in a solid.

Remember - the key word is testable. That is, you could perform a test of how two variables

f.   The woman opens her parachute. This force acts on the parachute to slow her down – air resistance
g.   The woman lands on the ground. This is the force of the ground pushing against her weight – reaction

Introducing variables

Variables are things in an experiment that can change or be controlled, There are three types of variables:

(@) an independent variable what you change; that is, the variable you are testing, which should be
the only thing you change in an experiment

(b) a dependent variable ~ what you measure; that is, the variable that changes depending on the
value of the independent variable

(©) a controlled variable ~ what you keep the same so that you can be sure any change to the
dependent variable is caused by changes to the independent variable. If you do not keep these
other variables the same, you won’t know which variable has affected your results

Wave Worksheet

In order to see sound wave more easily, scientists use a piece of equipment called a cathode ray
oscilloscope to convert a longitudinal sound wave into a digital transverse wave.




Frequency – The frequency of a wave is how many times it vibrates in one second. Frequency is measured
in Hertz (Hz). The higher the frequency of a vibration, the higher the pitch of the sound that is produced.

Amplitude – The amplitude measures the energy of a transverse wave. It is measured from the resting
position to the top of a crest or the bottom of a trough. The higher the amplitude, the louder the sound
that is produced. The loudness of sounds is measured in Decibels (Db).

Writing up a Practical Report


Scientists write up the results of their experiments and observations in
a practical report. The following headings are often used in a practical
report:

Aim - states the problem or purpose of the experiment. Often the hypothesis is stated as the aim.

Equipment - a list of the apparatus used in the experiment

Method - a step-by-step list of what was done in the experiment. This is written in the past tense and in
sufficient detail so that someone else could repeat the experiment.

Diagrams - showing how the apparatus was set up are often used. Completed in pencil and it is labelled with
arrows.

Results/Observations - shows your observations and measurements, often presented in a table or as a graph.

Conclusion - this is the answer to the aim or problem being investigated. States what happened, supports it
with evidence and explains why: scientific understandings

CHAPTER 11: The Mole

In Science, as previously mentioned, the mass of single atoms is far too small to be of
practical value. However, masses must be used in calculations, hence masses based
on Atomic (and Formula) Masses are used.

Consider the elements aluminium and carbon —

Atomic mass of aluminium _ 27
Atomic mass of carbon 12
ie the mass of 1 atom of aluminium _ 27
: the mass of 1 atom of carbon 12
the mass of 2 atoms of aluminium —~ 24X27 _ 7
the mass of 2 atoms of carbon 2x12 12
and the mass of 10 atoms of aluminium — 10x27 _ 27
the mass of 10 atoms of carbon 10x12 ~ 12
the mass of N atoms of aluminium _ NX 27 _, 27
. the mass of N atoms of carbon NX12 42

Whenever the number of aluminium and carbon atoms is the same the ratio of the
mass of aluminium to the mass of carbon will be 27:12.

Therefore, if we take 27g of aluminium and 12g of carbon, each sample must contain
the same number of atoms

Similarly, if we take 1g of hydrogen or 14g of nitrogen, we must have the same
number of atoms in each sample as there are atoms of carbon in a 12g sample of car-
bon.

That is, whenever we take a sample of an element which has a mass equal to its
Atomic Mass expressed in grams we have the same number of atoms in that sample
as there are atoms of carbon in a 12g sample of carbon.

The very large number of atoms contained in such a sample is called Avogadro's
Number.

Avogadro’s Number = 6,02 X 10% (approximately)

Similarly it can be shown that Avogadro’s number of molecules of a substance has a
mass which is equal to its Formula Mass expressed in grams.

Avogadro’s Number (6.02 X 10?) of particles of a substance is known as a MOLE of
that substance.

2, A MOLE of a substance is that quantity of that substance which has a mass
equal to its atomic (or formula) mass expressed in grams.
